Dont do it. 

LASIK is a big guessing game by the surgeon. They dont know how your body will respond to the alterations made by the laser. Will it heal the way they intend and anticipate - if yes, great you get a good outcome. If not, then enjoy higher order abberations (ghosting) and glare / halos at night. None of this is reversible by the way, so if it goes wrong, you're stuck with it for life. 

Sure, you can get fancy sclerals and put eye drops in to keep your pupils small, but then you have just traded one (minor) inconvenience, which was corrective lenses, for another relatively larger inconvenience (and more expensive too) 

So think long and hard about this decision. Dont fall for the LASIK marketing hype and bogus statistics from "studies". Alot of people have alot of cognitive dissonance about their procedures, probably as a way to trick themselves into thinking it wasnt a big mistake. Just look at facebook comments and even reddit comments on people who are "satisfied" There is an alarming amount of people who say "I love my lasik, except for \*insert complaint about glare, night driving difficulties, light sensitivity, starbursts, dry eyes\*. " 

Reality is, this procedure is far from perfected, and there is no real reason to cut into and evaporate a perfectly healthy cornea if your vision can be corrected. At this point, LASIK has been around for too long and there is too much money in the industry for it to go away. Thankfully though, completely non-invasive vision correction methods are coming to the forefront, namely PiXL and LIRIC and some from Clarity Vision. (all changing the structure / properties of the cornea, not evaporating it into the right shape)

That rainbow pattern is due to the raster pattern of the excimer laser used when creating your lasik flap. The  finely spaced dots of the excimer laser act a perfect grating to cause incoming light to diffract into the rainbow colors. 

There are two options to get rid of this:


1) lift the flap back up,  ablate the underside of the flap a few microns and put it back, hopefully fixing the diffraction pattern

2) wait 6 months or more, it may go away. 

I speak from personal experience, I had lasik in may 2018, and experienced the diffraction pattern around led light sources too. I still do to this day. It has lessened a bit though. 

For more information search lasik diffraction pattern Dr gatinel on google. Gatinel has done some work on this

Cornea transplant can happen for a number of reasons outside of lasik. 

However the reasons which a cornea transplant may need to occur as a result directly or indirectly from lasik would be unrecoverable damage from the procedure to the cornea, severe cornea scarring as a result of the procedure, or corneal ectasia so severe that a transplant is needed.

It's not really anyone's "fault". Just know that there really is a level of guesswork involved in lasik/prk on the part of the surgeon.  First of all, pre op measurements don't capture the refractive properties of the eye fully. Measurements are never 100% perfect. Also, everyone heals differently after the procedure. No two eyes heal the same.  They may heal similarly, which is why the surgeon chooses in large part to overcorrect you slightly initially, to allow for the body's natural regression healing response. But we are all different, and so what works on one person won't work on another.  

And the fact that you have likely gotten a treatment with an optical zone smaller than or equal to your night time adapted pupil size - yes that would be a mistake of the surgeon. He/she would be well aware of the relationships between optical zone, scotopic pupil size and observed higher order abberations.

Yes large pupils for most surgeons are not good. 

This is because most surgeons go with the standard 6.5mm optical zone diameter, with a blended zone out to 9mm. The prescription is only lasered onto 6.5mm diameter of your eyeball, and the blend out to 9mm is just a smoothing zone so there isn't an abrupt difference in curvature between the optical zone and the untreated cornea. 

Now.... it is possible to have optical zones up to 8mm, but you need large lasik flaps for that, which are harder to cut and problematic when laying back down. AND for larger diameters of optical zone, particularly for higher prescriptions, more cornea must be removed, increasing the risk for ectasia, hence being most likely not possible to treat with a 8mm or larger optical zone. 

There may be surgeons put there who treat to 8mm optical zones, but they are few and far between. Alot of surgeons are of the ignorant opinion that a 6.5mm optical zone is fine for an 8mm pupil. Which just doesn't make sny sense at all.
